title: The Design (Module 6B, lesson 29)
summary: Design is a plan or drawing showing the appearance of something before it is made; in embroidery it is a decorative pattern that adds beauty to an article. Choose a design suited to age, sex, occasion and need (a bright red heavily decorated saree is wrong for a summer wedding with a baby). Five types: geometrical (lines, circles, squares, rectangles, triangles; e.g. a hut), simplified (slight curves and few details), naturalized (close to nature: flowers, leaves, birds), stylised (more curves and details, away from the natural form, more decorative and complicated) and abstract (no specific inspiration; uses only the texture, veins, pattern or colour of an object). A leaf can be shown as naturalized, simplified, stylised and abstract.
A design starts with a motif; when a motif is repeated at certain intervals over a surface it is called a pattern; repetition of the pattern creates a design.

A design may have to be enlarged or reduced to suit the article (a big flower on a diwan cover, a small one on a cushion cover). Steps: find the design, trace it on tracing paper, transfer the tracing with carbon paper to graph paper, then use the squares as a guide to draw it on larger squares (enlargement) or smaller squares (reduction); each part increases by the same amount in width and height so proportion is kept.
## Selecting a design and planning the article

Factors: purpose (cartoons on children's wear), shape and size of the article, colour and texture of the fabric (light embroidery on delicate chiffon, heavy on thick cotton), occasion, sex and age of the wearer, effective use of the fabric background, decorating points of emphasis (collar, pocket, neckline) and comfort (not heavy or abrasive to the skin). Plan the article by asking who will use it, what for, where, when and how; e.g. an eco-friendly shopping bag needs light, strong, water-resistant, colour-fast, non-snagging fabric (canvas, jute, cotton), strong handles, bright colours suited to all ages and embroidery in proportion to the bag.

Six methods: (1) direct (free-hand pencil on thin or transparent fabrics such as lawn, organdie, georgette, with the fabric tight in a hoop); (2) carbon paper (carbon side down between fabric and design, trace with a dry ball pen; use white or yellow carbon on dark fabric and blue on light or white); (3) back tracing (draw on tracing paper, go over the back of the lines with 2B or 4B pencil, tape with the pencilled side to the fabric and trace; simplest, no costly equipment; for symmetrical designs draw a quarter and fold); (4) butter paper or perforated pattern (trace on butter paper, prick holes along the lines with a needle or an empty sewing machine, pin on the fabric, rub with a ball of cotton dipped in a paste of powdered blue and kerosene oil, blow off the excess); (5) glass plate and light (glass over chair arms with a bulb below; design on thin paper under the fabric, outline with a hard pencil); (6) template (a shape cut from card paper, for simple designs repeated many times; draw the outline and remove).
Divide the measured garment into equal squares with tailor's chalk and place motifs: horizontal, vertical, half drop, diagonal or border placement.

objective: Identify the following methods of transferring designs with their descriptions: (i) Uses a glass plate and light to trace the design directly onto the fabric (ii) Involves tracing the design on butter paper and making small holes along it (iii) Drawing the design directly on the fabric with a pencil (iv) Uses carbon paper to transfer the design onto the fabric.
(i) Glass plate and light method. (ii) Butter paper (perforated pattern) method. (iii) Direct method. (iv) Carbon paper method.
State True or False. (a) A motif repeated over a surface gives a pattern. (b) Dark fabric needs blue carbon paper.
(a) True. (b) False: white or yellow carbon is used on dark fabric.
Match Column A with Column B. A: (a) Geometrical design (b) Abstract design. B: (i) Made of lines and shapes (ii) No specific inspiration (iii) Close to nature.
vsa: What is the main purpose of enlarging or reducing a design?
It lets one motif be used on articles of different sizes and shapes. The design size can then fit the size of the article.
How will you change a small design into a large design?
Trace the design, transfer it with carbon paper on graph paper and draw it on larger squares. Each part is enlarged equally in width and height.
Compare a geometrical design with an abstract design.
A geometrical design is built from lines and shapes like circles and squares. An abstract design has no specific inspiration and uses only texture, veins or colour of an object.
What four factors will you consider while selecting an embroidery design for a baby's frock?
The age of the baby so decorations like stones or zari that scratch should be avoided. Soft light fabric, comfort, safe thread and a simple naturalized or simplified design (and bright colours).
Give two comparisons between stylised and geometrical design.

Stylised designs have more curves and details and are away from natural form; geometrical designs use simple shapes and straight lines. Stylised designs look decorative and complicated while geometrical ones look simple.
Differentiate between a motif and a pattern.
A motif is the basic unit of a design. A pattern is made by repeating the motif at intervals.
sa: Describe any two methods of transferring a design from paper onto fabric.

(i) Carbon paper: place carbon face down between fabric and design and trace with a dry ball pen. (ii) Back tracing: go over the back of the lines of a tracing with a 2B pencil, tape it to the fabric and trace the lines with the back of a pencil.
List the factors to consider while selecting a design for a frock for a three-year-old niece (three points).

(i) It should suit her age: soft fabric, light embroidery and no stones or zari that scratch. (ii) Simple naturalized or cartoon designs in bright colours with safe threads. (iii) The size should suit the frock and embroidery should be at points of emphasis.
Explain the five types of designs briefly.

(i) Geometrical designs use shapes and lines and simplified designs use slight curves with few details. (ii) Naturalized designs are close to nature. (iii) Stylised designs are decorative with more curves; abstract designs have no specific inspiration.
Explain the factors to be considered while planning an eco-friendly shopping bag.

(i) It must be light but strong with strong handles. (ii) The fabric must be water resistant, colour fast and non-absorbent such as canvas or jute. (iii) The embroidery must not snag and should suit all age groups.
la: Explain the six methods of transferring a design on a fabric.

(i) Direct method: freehand pencil on thin fabrics like georgette. (ii) Carbon paper: trace with a dry ball pen, using white carbon on dark fabric. (iii) Back tracing: pencil the back of a tracing and trace over it. (iv) Butter paper: prick holes along the lines and rub with a paste of blue powder in kerosene. (v) Glass plate and light: outline with a hard pencil over a bulb under glass. (vi) Template: card paper shape traced for repeated simple designs.
